question: Should I keep doing the bowel screening test every two years?

source.title: Bowel cancer screening: what the test can and can't tell you
source.publisher: Test fixture written for this repo (numbers are illustrative)
quotes: It is offered every two years to people aged 50 to 74.
Out of 1,000 people aged 50 to 74, about 30 will develop bowel cancer over the next 25 years if none of them is screened.
Over 25 years, screening every two years finds roughly 60% of the cancers that would develop, early enough to treat more easily.
Each time someone does the test, about 5 in 100 get a positive result.
Over many rounds of screening, about a third of people who keep screening will get at least one positive result.
In fact, fewer than 1 in 20 positive results turn out to be cancer.
Doing the test regularly matters more than doing it once.

ask.question: How many of the home tests will you do between 50 and 74?
ask.help: One test is posted to you every two years, so 13 in all.

ask.question: If a test came back positive, would you have the colonoscopy?
ask.help: A colonoscopy is a camera check of the bowel, done in hospital.

explain.caption: Out of 100 people your age, who gets bowel cancer?
A few of them will get bowel cancer over 25 years.
Every two years, each person posts a small sample.
A positive result means the test found traces of blood.
A positive result leads to a colonoscopy, a camera check.
Some colonoscopies find cancer early, when it is easier to treat.
But most positive results turn out not to be cancer.
Skip tests, and fewer cancers are found early.
So cancers that aren't found keep growing unseen.
Now make it yours. Answer two quick questions.

simulate.prompt: Try fewer tests, or skipping a colonoscopy, and watch the crowds.

tradeoffs: More tests find more cancers early, but also mean more positive results that turn out to be nothing.
A colonoscopy can find cancer early, but it is uncomfortable and carries a small risk.
The home test is simple and private, but a negative result does not rule cancer out.
Doing every test takes a few minutes every two years, while skipping tests leaves gaps where a cancer can grow unseen.
leftOut: The numbers in this article are illustrative, so check the figures for your own country's program.
Your own risk can be higher or lower than average, for example with a family history of bowel cancer.
The model assumes each test you do finds the same share of cancers; in real life the timing of tests matters.
How often people get a second positive result is an assumption, chosen so about a third get at least one.
It leaves out the small risks of colonoscopy itself, and cancers that appear between tests.
Symptoms matter whatever your last test said: the model does not cover them.
